title: How Brain-Computer Interfaces Can Read Your Thoughts

shots.vo: Right now, roughly eighty-six billion neurons in your brain are firing tiny electrical signals. Every thought, every movement you plan, every word you're about to say starts as a pattern of these sparks.
Each neuron connects to thousands of others, forming something like a hundred trillion connections. It's the most complex network we know of in the universe.
What if a machine could listen in? Not just to notice that your brain is busy, but to understand what it's trying to do?

That's the idea behind brain-computer interfaces. And they're no longer science fiction. People who can't move or speak are already using them to control computers, robotic arms, and even to talk again. So how do they work? And can they really read your thoughts?

Neurons communicate with electrical pulses called spikes, each lasting about a thousandth of a second. When you decide to move your hand, neurons in a strip of your brain called the motor cortex fire in a specific pattern.
If you can record that pattern, and learn what it means, you can turn intention into action, even when the body can no longer carry it out.

Scientists have known about this strip for a long time. In the mid-twentieth century, the Canadian surgeon Wilder Penfield gently stimulated patients' brains during surgery, and mapped which spots made the hand, face, or foot twitch.
The simplest way to listen is from outside the head. In 1924, the German psychiatrist Hans Berger recorded the first human brain waves using electrodes on the scalp. Today we call it EEG.
EEG is safe and cheap, but the skull blurs the signal. It's like trying to follow a conversation inside a stadium from outside the walls. You hear the roar, but not the words.

There's a middle ground, too. Some electrodes sit on the surface of the brain, under the skull, but without piercing it. Patients with epilepsy sometimes have these placed for monitoring, and many have volunteered for brain-computer interface experiments.

To hear individual neurons, you have to go inside. One of the most widely used devices is the Utah array: a tiny square of a hundred needle-like electrodes, about four millimeters across, placed into the surface of the brain.
Electrodes inside the brain can pick up the spikes of individual nearby neurons. But it means brain surgery, so these devices have mainly been tested in people with severe paralysis.

One of the first implants was placed in 1998, by the neurologist Philip Kennedy. A man named Johnny Ray, unable to move or speak after a stroke, learned to move a cursor on a screen with his brain signals.
In 2006, a paralyzed man named Matthew Nagle used one to move a computer cursor, just by thinking about moving his hand. It was part of a research program called BrainGate.

In 2012, Cathy Hutchinson, who had been paralyzed by a stroke, used a robotic arm controlled by her brain to pick up a bottle of coffee and drink from it. It was the first time in about fifteen years that she had served herself a drink.

Later systems even added a sense of touch. In 2016, Nathan Copeland, paralyzed in a car accident, controlled a robotic arm whose fingers sent signals back into his brain, so he could feel what it touched. He even fist-bumped President Obama.

The secret is decoding. Computers learn to match patterns of brain activity to intended movements. At first, the person imagines specific movements while the computer records. Over many sessions, the software and the person's brain adapt to each other.

In 2021, researchers at Stanford asked a paralyzed man to imagine writing letters by hand. An AI turned his brain activity into text at about ninety characters per minute, approaching how fast many people type on a phone.

Today's decoders often use the same kinds of artificial neural networks that power speech recognition on your phone. They learn the subtle patterns linking thousands of signals to what the person is trying to do.

params.words: i can finally tell you what i am thinking

shots.vo: Then came speech. In 2023, two teams published breakthroughs side by side. A woman with ALS, who could no longer speak clearly, communicated at sixty-two words per minute.

Speech devices work by listening to the brain area that controls the lips, tongue, jaw and voice box. An AI decodes the intended sounds, and a language model, like a supercharged autocorrect, turns them into likely words and sentences.

params.words: hello it is so good to hear my voice

shots.vo: Another woman, paralyzed by a stroke eighteen years earlier, spoke at seventy-eight words per minute through a digital avatar that moved its face, with a voice based on a recording from her wedding.

params.sub: accuracy turning attempted speech into words (2024)
params.sub2: spoken in a voice recreated from his old recordings

shots.vo: In 2024, a man with ALS named Casey Harrell used an implant that turned his attempted speech into words with about ninety-seven percent accuracy, read aloud in a voice recreated from old recordings of his own.

params.words: normal conversation is about one hundred and sixty words per minute

shots.vo: Normal conversation runs at about a hundred and sixty words per minute. These systems aren't there yet. But for people who were trapped in silence, being able to joke, argue, and say I love you again is life-changing.
Companies are now racing to make these devices practical. Neuralink's implant is about the size of a coin, with over a thousand electrodes on ultra-thin threads, inserted by a surgical robot.

In 2024, its first patient, Noland Arbaugh, paralyzed from the shoulders down, used it to move a cursor and play chess and video games. Some threads later pulled out of his brain, but software changes restored much of the performance.
Another company, Synchron, takes a different route. Its device is threaded up through a blood vessel and expands inside a vein next to the motor cortex, with no need to open the skull.

And in 2023, Swiss researchers connected a man's brain implants to an implant on his spinal cord. Paralyzed after a bike accident, he was able to walk again, more naturally than before, just by thinking about it.

And some interfaces send signals the other way. Cochlear implants turn sound into electrical pulses that stimulate the hearing nerve. More than a million people use them to hear, making them by far the most successful neural interface so far.
So can these devices read your thoughts? Not the way it sounds. Most brain-computer interfaces decode intended movements or attempted speech, from the specific brain areas that control them.
But scientists are getting closer. In 2023, researchers in Texas used brain scans to decode the general meaning of stories people were listening to, or even just imagining, without any implant.

lines: the gist, not word for word
params.sub: ~16 hours of training per person · failed when people resisted

shots.vo: It wasn't word for word. It needed about sixteen hours of training data for each person. And it stopped working when people resisted, for example by deliberately thinking about something else.
Still, it raises serious questions. Brain data could reveal your intentions, your emotions, even early signs of disease. Who owns that data, and who gets to see it?

params.sub: some US states now protect neural data too

shots.vo: In 2021, Chile became the first country to protect brain activity and mental privacy in its constitution. Some US states have since passed laws to protect neural data as well.
There are physical risks too. Brain surgery can cause infection and bleeding, and implants can lose signal over time as the brain's tissue reacts to a foreign object.
And brain data isn't only collected in hospitals. Consumer headbands that read EEG are already sold for meditation, sleep, and focus, gathering signals from people's brains every day.
For now, brain-computer interfaces are mostly about restoring what was lost: movement, communication, independence.
In the future, they may help treat conditions like depression, epilepsy, or blindness. Some people even imagine using them to enhance healthy brains, though that's much further off.

vo: Brain-computer interfaces can't read your mind like a book. But they can listen to what you're trying to say, and help you say it. For people who've lost their voice, that's nothing short of extraordinary.
